description: Cryptographic Agility Assessment Framework across 7 core dimensions

C1.name: Operation Coupling
C1.description: Degree to which cryptographic operations (signing, encrypting, hashing) are hardcoded at invocation call sites.

levels.0: Hardcoded algorithm and parameter calls directly scattered across business logic functions.
levels.1: Calls use direct algorithm classes but reference localized utility helper functions.
levels.2: Cryptographic operations invoke service-level abstraction wrappers with fixed parameter sets.
levels.3: Operations use generic crypto facades/interfaces where algorithm is passed via method parameters.
levels.4: Fully decoupled: business logic consumes domain-level security intents (e.g. secure_payload, verify_identity) without referencing algorithms.

C2.name: Creation Coupling
C2.description: How cryptographic keys, certificates, and cipher contexts are instantiated.

levels.0: Keys and contexts are directly instantiated naming concrete algorithms (e.g., rsa.generate_private_key).
levels.1: Direct instantiation isolated to a dedicated module but without parameterized factory.
levels.2: Factory pattern used with hardcoded switch cases for supported algorithms.
levels.3: Dynamic factory pattern using service providers or dependency injection with external configuration.
levels.4: Full KMS / HSM / PKCS#11 key abstraction where key handles are referenced without algorithmic binding in source.

C3.name: Provider Coupling
C3.description: Coupling to underlying cryptographic library or hardware provider implementation.

levels.0: Direct vendor/library proprietary API imports tightly coupled throughout codebase (e.g. proprietary C extensions).
levels.1: Coupled to a standard platform library (e.g., Python cryptography, Node.js crypto, Java JCA) with direct class imports.
levels.2: Standard library wrapped behind internal application adapters.
levels.3: Pluggable provider architecture allowing provider swap via standard interfaces (e.g., JCA Security.addProvider).
levels.4: Hardware-agnostic and provider-agnostic abstraction supporting transparent HSM/TPM/Software failover.

C4.name: Decoupling Mechanism
C4.description: Mechanism required to transition to a new algorithm or parameter set.

levels.0: Full code rewrite, re-compilation, and database schema migration required.
levels.1: Code change limited to central constants/configuration classes, but requires recompilation and redeployment.
levels.2: Static configuration file change (e.g., YAML/JSON/ENV) requiring service restart.
levels.3: Dynamic runtime configuration reloadable via hot-reload/API without service restart.
levels.4: Dynamic policy-driven negotiation where client and server autonomously negotiate supported PQC/classical algorithms.

C5.name: Decoupling Authority
C5.description: Who or what has authority to modify cryptographic algorithms and posture.

levels.0: Individual developer discretion at code write time with no centralized policy enforcement.
levels.1: Ad-hoc code review process without automated policy checks.
levels.2: Development team leads control configuration files per service.
levels.3: Centralized enterprise security configuration repository with automated CI/CD policy linting.
levels.4: Centralized enterprise cryptographic policy engine with real-time posture enforcement and automated migration orchestration.

E1.name: Algorithm Migration Capability
E1.description: Capability of the system data structures and protocols to accommodate PQC algorithm characteristics (e.g., larger public keys and ciphertexts).

levels.0: Fixed buffer sizes, strict database column limits (e.g. VARCHAR(256)), or rigid wire protocols that break with large PQC keys.
levels.1: Variable buffer sizes in memory, but serialized protocol formats or database schemas enforce rigid length constraints.
levels.2: Database supports arbitrary blobs, but network transport/API schemas (e.g. HTTP headers) enforce size restrictions.
levels.3: Data structures and network transport accommodate large public keys (e.g. ML-KEM-768: 1184 bytes, ML-DSA-65: 1952 bytes) with minor adjustments.
levels.4: Fully protocol-agile: supports hybrid and standalone PQC key exchange/signatures with transparent chunking and parameter negotiation.

E2.name: Provider Migration Capability
E2.description: Readiness to switch or augment underlying cryptographic providers (e.g. adding liboqs, Bouncy Castle PQC, or AWS KMS PQC).

levels.0: Tightly bound to a single legacy provider that offers no PQC roadmap.
levels.1: Using standard provider that currently lacks PQC, requiring library replacement for migration.
levels.2: Using standard provider with planned PQC support in upcoming versions (e.g., OpenSSL 3.x, Bouncy Castle 1.78+).
levels.3: Dual-provider architecture or wrapper capable of binding a PQC sidecar / hybrid provider alongside classical.
levels.4: Modular plug-and-play provider architecture with verified compatibility across classical, hybrid, and NIST PQC FIPS standard libraries.
